extracted.intended_audience: computer scientists and mathematicians (graduate students, researchers, and technical authors) who write papers, expository articles, and textbooks
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and publishing mathematical/computer-science papers, expository articles, and textbooks for both specialist and general audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make pieces accessible to the intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing for a general audience (e.g., Scientific American), remove jargon and simplify exposition so non-specialists can follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: SA editors removed technical jargon from Don's article; Martin Gardner attributes success to writers who are not deep specialists. Don eventually agreed editors helped remove jargon. Balance simplification with technical accuracy; expect editors to reword heavily when preparing for a general reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for—and collaborate with—editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial changes are common (rewriting sentences, changing voice, punctuation, word choice); authors should review edits and negotiate where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don received heavy edits from SA, then later re-edited and negotiated at the proof stage. Some editor changes can introduce errors, so authors should inspect proofs carefully and politely argue for corrections (e.g., restoring mathematical symbols or specific wording).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect and correct page proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many errors and formatting problems appear only at the page-proof stage; authors should review proofs to catch symbol substitutions, line breaks, and layout problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '1' changed to 'l', '∅' to 'ϕ', paragraph breaks that isolate a single last line, brackets replacing floor brackets. Don negotiated changes in a 1.5-hour phone call and got some corrections after proofs were sent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve mathematical notation and typography
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain correct mathematical symbols and typographic conventions; printers/typesetters unfamiliar with math may substitute wrong symbols or not honor special brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: confusion of empty-set symbol, interchangeable use of brackets and parentheses in formulae despite differing meanings, replacement of floor brackets by square brackets. Insist on correct symbols in proofs and final copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt format to medium constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Different venues have different style and technical constraints (e.g., popular magazines may avoid displayed equations or limit technical detail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientiﬁc American reportedly never displays equations; authors must find ways to convey ideas without heavy formalism in such venues. For journals that typeset formulas differently, request exceptions or proofs if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get readers' attention immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use snappy titles, arresting first sentences, and lucid initial paragraphs to engage readers quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf's advice: strong titles (e.g., 'Trisecting the Angle, the Heptagon, and the Triskaidecagon'), intriguing opening questions (e.g., 'Can a graph be continuous and discontinuous?'), or autobiographical hooks to draw readers in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-load: state purpose and results up front
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell readers plainly what the paper is about early so they can decide whether to read further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf: 'Get everything up front.' A clear plain-English summary can significantly increase readership. Provide a concise statement of main results near the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make papers scannable and highlight main results
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers often skim; make statements of theorems/results prominent (boldface or otherwise) and avoid dense inline notation in key statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use boldface or visual emphasis so page-flippers can find theorems. Drop convoluted notational abbreviations in theorem statements so skimmers can latch on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep motivation concise and effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide enough motivation to orient the reader, but avoid overlong motivational digressions; avoid many failed-example motivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A little motivation is good; repeated examples that don't succeed quickly lose charm. Wilf warns that many 'Consider the following...' setups are signals of contrived examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples abundantly and judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Good examples (simple then refined) convey most ideas and help readers form mental models, but examples must be carefully chosen to illustrate the intended points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman: 'I never saw a book with too many examples.' Present a simple example to convey the main idea and later refine with a complex example to show edge cases. Finding good examples is hard and worth the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep definitions and uses close together
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers learn better when definitions and their first uses appear near each other; do not bury definitions far from use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman notes readers don't refer back; repeat definitions when needed rather than forcing readers to flip pages. Repetition is acceptable to aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an exposition level appropriate to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance depth and accessibility: avoid opaque mechanics unless the audience can absorb them; choose how much background to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-off example: spend many pages on asymptotic analysis or simply state 'It can be shown that...' and refer to other texts. Ullman favored teaching the basics and avoiding deep proofs in some contexts to keep exposition accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style around proofs: informal framing, formal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Be chatty and motivating before and after proofs, and present the proofs in a lean, rigorous style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf: aim to be 'chatty' leading up to a proof, prove in a 'lean and mean' Rudin-like style, then be chatty again afterward. First-person usage is acceptable in exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: State types and be precise in language
rubrics_metrics.description: State the types/sets of variables explicitly and avoid ambiguous non-referential uses of words like 'this'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman: say 'the set S' rather than just 'S'; avoid 'this' unless referent is crystal-clear—misused 'this' can bewilder readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with grammatical/usage decisions that affect tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Some editorial style changes (e.g., data singular/plural, 'that' vs 'which', 'has' vs 'have') reflect interpretive choices; choose and defend consistent usage appropriate to audience and venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ACM changed 'data has' to 'data have'; Scientific American insisted on 'that' instead of 'which'; authors may contest or accept such changes depending on intent and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent and appropriate numeric formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Number formatting may differ between prose and formulas and across venues; be consistent and use the most appropriate form for context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Don used 1000000 in formulas; ACM substituted 1,000,000 in text; IEEE recommends spaces like '1 234 567' in numerical tables. Use scientific/exponent notation (e.g., 10^6) if more appropriate for formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose terminology and names thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and terminology can persist and influence perception; pick terms you won't regret where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don regretted some names (e.g., 'Daemon' vs 'Oracle'); others changed by community consensus (e.g., 'Polynomially-complete' → 'NP-complete'). Names may be altered later; consider community conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and consider alternative formats (dialog/Q&A) where effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Nontraditional formats (dialog, Q&A) can be effective exposition tools to present ideas intuitively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamport's and Don's dialog-format expositions (e.g., Surreal Numbers) and Lamport's Q&A in a technical report are cited as excellent examples—use dialogue when it clarifies flow and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt clear typographic conventions for formal material
rubrics_metrics.description: Use fonts and typographic conventions to distinguish formal elements (e.g., code, logic) from prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nilsson & Genesereth chapter uses a 'typewriter' font for logic. Establish consistent conventions (fonts for code/logic, italics for emphasis) to aid readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be rigorous about attribution; avoid plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not lift text or mathematical content verbatim without proper attribution; close imitation of structure/notation can be suspicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman: imitation becomes culpable if a reasonable person would think you had the other book open while writing. Identical sequences of equations or identical italics/notation are strong evidence. For survey papers, verbatim quotes are acceptable with clear attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use co-authors to improve quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-authors help filter idiosyncrasies and improve clarity, even if they don't save time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman: co-authors won't reduce workload but help keep the work grounded; filtering oddball material improves the book's marketability and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design a market/niche strategy for textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a market position (be the hardest, easiest, or best book on a topic) and aim for measurable sales targets to make book-writing worthwhile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman's commercial reasoning: target ~10k domestic sales; know your market; choose a young/booming field for bigger sales; prepare camera-ready copy to reduce publisher costs and improve royalty leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spend time finding and polishing effective examples
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality examples illustrate concepts clearly; invest significant time selecting and refining them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman: even a simple example conveys most of an idea; expand later with complex examples to cover edge cases. Good examples are a major determiner of pedagogical success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy and metaphor when they clarify
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy and metaphor can help exposition if readers will reliably get the point; use them where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman encourages analogy when sure it aids understanding; Don used biological metaphors (jellyfish, stems, polyps) to explain complex data-structure concepts in reductions—metaphor helped convey structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be selective about what to publish
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish because you have genuinely interesting results or are excited about the work—not to pad publication lists or just to appear in a particular venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamport warns against publishing for quantity or to get into a specific conference; choose to publish when the work merits dissemination. The 'best things left unpublished' may indicate judicious restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for detailed copyediting on captions and layout
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed venues may require line-length adjustments and caption rewriting to fit layout constraints; anticipate and edit captions for fit and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SA copy editors hand-tune caption linebreaks and sometimes remove words like 'the' to make lines fit. Know that such mechanical edits can consume editor time and affect other editorial tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate editorial changes tactfully and prioritize correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some editorial changes are stylistic, others affect correctness; focus negotiations on correctness and clarity while accepting some stylistic edits for audience fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don successfully argued some points (e.g., 'that' vs 'which') and failed on others ('commonest'). Prioritize restoring mathematical meaning and correctness; accept stylistic shifts where they improve accessibility.
